slides.title: Before the Second Chechen War
slides.body:
An Islamist incursion into Dagestan and apartment bombings in Russia preceded a renewed Russian invasion of separatist Chechnya.

The Conflict Takes Shape: Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims. The opening phase established the political goals, alliances, and military problems that shaped every later campaign.

stats.val: Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims.

slides.cap: Opening context for the Second Chechen War

slides.title: 1999 Russian apartment bombings
slides.body:
In September 1999, a series of explosions hit four apartment blocks in the Russian cities of Buynaksk, Moscow, and Volgodonsk, killing more than 300, injuring more than 1,000, and spreading a wave of fear across the country. The bombings, together with the 1999 war of Dagestan, triggered the Second Chechen War. The handling of the crisis by Vladimir Putin, who was prime minister at the time, boosted his popularity greatly and helped him attain the presidency within a few months.

Why This Moment Matters: 1999 Russian apartment bombings was more than an isolated engagement. It helped define the conflict's direction and exposed the strengths and weaknesses of the opposing sides. Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims.

slides.title: Consequences
slides.body: The effects of 1999 Russian apartment bombings extended beyond its immediate result. Urban destruction, disappearances, torture, terrorism, and counterinsurgency abuses deeply affected civilians across the North Caucasus. Its place in the wider campaign also influenced later military choices and political calculations.

slides.title: Battle of Grozny
slides.body:
The second battle of Grozny or Operation Wolf Hunt was the siege and assault of the Chechen capital Grozny by Russian forces, lasting from late 1999 to early 2000. The siege and assault on the city resulted in the near total destruction of the urban area. In 2003, the United Nations designated Grozny as the most destroyed city on Earth. The battle had a devastating impact on the civilian population. It is estimated that between 5,000 and 8,000 civilians were killed during the siege, making it the bloodiest episode of the Second Chechen War.

Why This Moment Matters: Battle of Grozny was more than an isolated engagement. It helped define the conflict's direction and exposed the strengths and weaknesses of the opposing sides. Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims.

slides.title: Novye Aldi massacre
slides.body: The Novye Aldi massacre was the mass murder of Chechen civilians on February 5, 2000, in which Russian forces went on a cleansing operation (zachistka), summarily executing dozens. The village had been cluster-bombed a day prior to the massacre, and local residents urged to come out for inspection the next day. Upon entering the village, Russian forces shot their victims with automatic fire at close range. The killings were accompanied by looting, rape, arson and robbery. As a result of the deadly rampage by Russian forces, up to 82 civilians were killed in the spree. Houses of civilians were burnt in an attempt to destroy evidence of summary executions and other crimes. Looting took place on a large scale and organised manner.

slides.title: Battle for Height 776
slides.body:
The Battle for Height 776, part of the larger Battle of Ulus-Kert, was an engagement in the Second Chechen War that took place during fighting for control of the Argun River gorge in the highland Shatoysky District of central Chechnya, between the villages of Ulus-Kert and Selmentauzen.

Why This Moment Matters: Battle for Height 776 was more than an isolated engagement. It helped define the conflict's direction and exposed the strengths and weaknesses of the opposing sides. Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims.

slides.title: Battle of Komsomolskoye
slides.body: The Battle of Komsomolskoye took place in Chechnya during the Second Chechen War. Beginning on 6 March 2000 and lasting until 24 March 2000, it resulted in the deaths of more than 50 Russian soldiers and hundreds of Chechen militants over the course of two weeks of siege warfare. An unknown number of civilians were killed in the fighting as well. The fighting resulted in the destruction of most of the Chechen separatist units commanded by Ruslan Gelayev. Scores of Chechens were taken prisoner by the Russian military, and only a few survived the ensuing Komsomolskoye massacre. Marked by fierce urban combat, the Battle of Komsomolskoye was the bloodiest of the entire conflict.

slides.title: Why This Moment Matters
slides.body:
Battle of Komsomolskoye was more than an isolated engagement. It reflected the changing balance of power and pushed the conflict closer to its eventual outcome. Russia sought permanent control and the destruction of separatist forces, while the insurgency increasingly adopted Islamist and regional aims.

Consequences: The effects of Battle of Komsomolskoye extended beyond its immediate result. Its place in the wider campaign also influenced later military choices and political calculations.

slides.title: Pankisi Gorge crisis
slides.body:
The Pankisi Gorge crisis was a geopolitical dispute between Russia and Georgia concerning the presence of armed Chechen separatists and jihadists in Georgia, that peaked in 2002.

slides.title: 2005 Nalchik raid
slides.body:
The 2005 raid on Nalchik was a raid by a large group of Islamic militants on Nalchik, in the Kabardino-Balkar Republic (KBR) of southern Russia, on 13 October 2005.

slides.title: Insurgency in Ingushetia
slides.body:
The Insurgency in Ingushetia began in 2007 as a spillover of then ongoing separatist conflict in Chechnya into neighbouring Ingushetia. The conflict has been described as a civil war by local human rights activists and opposition politicians; others have referred to it as an uprising. By mid-2009 Ingushetia had surpassed Chechnya as the most violent of the North Caucasus republics. However, by 2015 the insurgency in the Republic had greatly weakened, and the casualty toll declined substantially in the intervening years.

Why This Moment Matters: Insurgency in Ingushetia was more than an isolated engagement. It reflected the changing balance of power and pushed the conflict closer to its eventual outcome. title: International and Human Dimensions
sub: The wider impact of the Second Chechen War

slides.title: International Dimension
slides.body:
Foreign fighters joined parts of the insurgency, but Moscow largely prevented international involvement.

The Human Cost: Urban destruction, disappearances, torture, terrorism, and counterinsurgency abuses deeply affected civilians across the North Caucasus.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: How the Second Chechen War ended and what followed

slides.title: The End of the Second Chechen War
slides.body: Russia restored control through overwhelming force and a loyal Chechen government, while insurgency spread into neighboring republics before declining.
